question: A facilitator wants Claude to produce short prompts and summaries live during workshops, with participants waiting in the room. She standardises on the deepest-reasoning tier so that the material is always as good as it can be. What is the greatest risk?
options: A) The facilitator becomes reliant on having Claude available, so a session held somewhere without connectivity is harder to run.
B) The material becomes more detailed than a live workshop can absorb, so participants receive more text than they can read aloud.
C) The workshop material varies in tone between sessions, so participants attending more than one workshop notice the difference.
D) The answers take longer to come back than a room of waiting participants can tolerate, so the help is unusable in the moment.
correct_answers: D) The answers take longer to come back than a room of waiting participants can tolerate, so the help is unusable in the moment.
explanations: Dependence on connectivity is a sensible contingency to plan for, but it applies equally whichever tier she picks, so it is not the risk created by standardising on the deepest one.
Over-long output is a genuine annoyance, but it is fixed by asking for something shorter. It is not caused by the tier choice, and the facilitator can control length in the request itself.
Some variation between sessions is expected with any tier and matters little for workshop prompts. It is a consistency preference rather than something that stops the session working.

Correct. Depth is bought with time, and in a live setting responsiveness is the binding constraint. Choosing the deepest tier here sacrifices the very quality, immediacy, that made Claude useful in the room.
